title: Time and the Conways

title: Boy

It is a prose fiction work of 1931 by James Hanley; it belongs to The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel and it is catalogued here under Proletarian Novel and the Working-Class Fiction; Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Thirteen-year-old Francis Ferris is taken from his brutal father and sent to sea as a cabin boy; the voyage of the SS Trevithick through the Suez Canal to the Far East becomes an ordeal of beatings, hunger and sexual exploitation, and the novel ends with his death in a dockside brothel.
narrative_structure: A novel in three parts, from Liverpool to the sea and the brothel. A novel in chapters of the workplace and the strike, the collective subject carried through the vernacular of the shop floor. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.
principal_characters: Francis Ferris; Mr Ferris; the captain; the crew of the SS Trevithick
literary_form: Novel; proletarian novel, first issued in 1931
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the proletarian novel: the vernacular of the workplace and the picket line, the documentary detail of wage, rent, hunger and the strike, and the collective rather than the individual subject. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, harsh, unadorned prose.
historical_context: Liverpool and the merchant navy in the late 1920s, and the poverty of the English working class. The record dates the work as composed between 1929 and 1931 and first published in 1931 and the corpus places it within The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel, it is catalogued under proletarian novel and the working-class fiction; experimental novel and the modernist form.
literary_significance: Boy is the most brutal English novel of the thirties: its unsparing prose and its treatment of the working-class child at sea made it a landmark of the proletarian novel, and it was banned and prosecuted on publication.

title: The Furys

title: Of Human Bondage
description: The great English novel of obsession: Philip Carey, Mildred, and the long education of a young man. It is a prose fiction work of 1915 by W. Somerset Maugham; it is catalogued here under Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind; Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Philip Carey, born with a club foot, is orphaned and raised by his uncle, the vicar of Blackstable; he studies in Germany, fails as an accountant and a painter, qualifies as a doctor in London, and destroys himself for the waitress Mildred Rogers before he finds his own life.
narrative_structure: A novel in three parts, from the orphanage to the medical practice and the marriage. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes.
principal_characters: Philip Carey; Mildred Rogers; Sally Athelny; Cronshaw; Hayward; Griffiths; Emma
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The author's characteristic manner is the first-person narrator who listens rather than judges.
